content: The youngest and most critically ill patients, as well as those who demonstrate adherence to treatment and can be monitored for adverse events, should be prioritized for care. However, patients who face socioeconomic barriers to adherence or reside in remote, rural, or underserved communities lacking the technical resources for treatment monitoring may be disproportionately disadvantaged. This inequity is unjust and requires attention. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized that injectable-sparing regimens are more feasible to decentralize, making them particularly suitable for remote and underserved settings. These regimens could help reduce health inequities without compromising treatment outcomes across different populations. Additionally, the absence of a requirement for audiometry in these regimens simplifies monitoring, even though electrocardiography (ECG) is necessary for the use of bedaquiline-containing regimens. The GDG stressed that ECG monitoring should not be a differentiating factor between regimens, as patients receiving injectable agents like amikacin also require regular cardiac monitoring. The GDG acknowledged that not all patients in certain settings may have access to ECG monitoring. However, they noted that increasing access to ECG at peripheral healthcare levels could improve equity in care delivery. A cost-effectiveness model was developed to evaluate the intervention, incorporating health system costs, drug procurement, healthcare delivery, adverse events, retreatments, secondary cases, and morbidity and mortality associated with tuberculosis (TB). In South Africa, the 9–12-month all-oral regimen was found to be both cost-saving and more effective than the shorter injectable-containing regimen under most modeled conditions. The projected cost savings averaged $1,000 per patient, depending on the balance between higher drug costs and reduced costs for injectable delivery and managing recurrent or secondary cases. In scenarios where the all-oral regimen was no longer cost-saving due to significantly higher bedaquiline prices, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio was still favorable, at $400 per disability-adjusted life year averted. A qualitative study involving key stakeholders, including patients and civil society representatives, revealed that most patients prioritize regimens with fewer and less severe side effects, as these allow them to maintain their daily activities. Survivors of drug-resistant TB expressed a willingness to accept longer treatment durations if it meant fewer severe adverse effects, even if the treatment was experimental or its efficacy uncertain. Conversely, a smaller group preferred shorter regimens with potentially more severe side effects to achieve a quicker return to normal life. The GDG noted that patient preferences are highly individual and context-dependent. However, a shorter, injection-free regimen with minimal physical and mental health side effects and a low pill burden was generally the most acceptable option. The implementation of the all-oral regimen may face challenges due to the need for improved laboratory infrastructure. While rapid molecular tests for rifampicin resistance are being implemented, countries must strengthen their capacity for genotypic and phenotypic testing of other agents in the regimen. Monitoring for the development of bedaquiline resistance is also critical, given its central role in new anti-TB regimens. The removal of injectable agents offers significant advantages, including reduced pain and adverse events for patients and greater convenience for healthcare workers. However, successful implementation requires sustainable system changes, including uninterrupted drug supply, active TB drug safety monitoring, and integration with existing pharmacovigilance systems. The GDG recommended a shorter, all-oral, bedaquiline-containing regimen of 9–12 months for eligible patients with confirmed multidrug-resistant or rifampin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) who have not been exposed to second-line TB medicines in this regimen for more than one month and in whom fluoroquinolone resistance has been excluded. This recommendation is conditional due to very low certainty in the evidence and the need for laboratory capacity and drug susceptibility testing (DST). The GDG recognized that the evidence supporting the efficacy of the all-oral regimen is limited and based on observational data. However, the regimen demonstrated a better success-to-unfavorable outcome ratio and reduced loss to follow-up. Cost-effectiveness modeling also showed robust savings compared to longer oral regimens or shorter injectable-containing regimens. Subgroup considerations included people living with HIV (PLHIV), where the regimen performed well in settings with high HIV prevalence. However, potential drug interactions, particularly those increasing bedaquiline exposure or cardiotoxicity, must be carefully managed when co-administered with antiretrovirals.
